title: Jeremiah 3:1–11
context: Jeremiah 3:1–5 continues the LORD’s covenant lawsuit from chapter 2. The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, opening with a legal question that alludes to the divorce law of Deuteronomy 24:1–4: a man who has put away his wife may not take her back after she has become another man’s. Judah has gone further than that case, yet the LORD still says “return again to me” (3:1). The marriage and prostitution imagery is covenant language for idolatry and political alliances, not a description of individuals. In 3:4–5 the LORD quotes the people’s easy words of piety and sets them against their deeds. A new unit begins at 3:6, which Jeremiah dates to “the days of Josiah the king” (compare 1:2): the LORD speaks to Jeremiah about two sisters, “backsliding Israel” (the northern kingdom) and “treacherous Judah.” Israel’s “certificate of divorce” (3:8) is commonly read as the northern kingdom’s fall to Assyria (2 Kings 17), and Judah’s return “only in pretense” (3:10) is often linked, with some caution, to a reform under Josiah (2 Kings 22–23) that did not reach the people’s hearts. Ezekiel 23 develops a similar two-sisters image by reference, in its own way. In 3:11 the LORD concludes that Israel has shown herself more righteous than Judah, preparing the call to return in 3:12. Arminian and Reformed readers share the conviction that covenant unfaithfulness is real guilt and that the LORD’s invitation to return is sincere; they differ, as elsewhere, on how grace brings about that return.

verses.text: “They say, ‘If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him, and becomes another man’s, should he return to her again?’ Wouldn’t that land be greatly polluted? But you have played the prostitute with many lovers; yet return again to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD frames Judah’s guilt with the divorce law of Deuteronomy 24:1–4, under which a husband could not take back a wife who had been another man’s. Arminian readers stress that the LORD nevertheless says “return again to me,” an invitation that goes beyond what the law permits and shows a genuine, open offer of mercy that Judah is truly able, by grace, to answer or refuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the LORD’s mercy surpassing the legal case: what no human husband could lawfully do, the LORD offers to do. They hear in “return again to me” a call grounded in covenant faithfulness that God himself will make effective in his people. Shared ground: both read the imagery as covenant idolatry, and both see grace exceeding law here.

verses.text: “Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been lain with? You have sat waiting for them by the road, as an Arabian in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your prostitution and with your wickedness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD points to the bare heights, places of idolatrous worship, and pictures Judah waiting for lovers like a desert traveler waiting by the road. Arminian readers note that the charge assumes real responsibility: Judah has sought other gods eagerly and freely, and the indictment is meant to awaken conscience so that she will turn back while the door remains open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same eagerness as evidence of a heart bent away from God, which pursues idols as naturally as a traveler watches the road. The verse diagnoses the depth of sin that only grace can reach. Shared ground: both traditions keep the imagery sober and covenantal, and both see that Judah’s idolatry has polluted the land itself.

verses.text: Therefore the showers have been withheld and there has been no latter rain; yet you have had a prostitute’s forehead and you refused to be ashamed.
verses.arminianNotes: Withheld showers and the missing latter rain are covenant warnings (compare Deuteronomy 11:13–17; 28:23–24). Arminian readers see such chastening as a merciful summons meant to lead Judah to repentance, and they note that the tragedy lies in the response: Judah has a brazen forehead and refuses to be ashamed when correction comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see drought as the covenant Lord’s discipline, governed by his providence and meant to humble. They note that outward hardship alone did not soften Judah, which underscores the need for an inward work of grace. Shared ground: both traditions hold that God disciplines his people, and that refusing shame is itself part of the guilt named here.

verses.text: Will you not from this time cry to me, ‘My Father, you are the guide of my youth!’?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether Judah will now cry “My Father, you are the guide of my youth!” Arminian readers often hear this as the LORD voicing the words Judah might sincerely pray, a real opening for return. Others take it as a quotation of Judah’s glib piety, which the next verse exposes. Either way, the relationship is offered as genuinely restorable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the cry, together with 3:5, as Judah’s easy speech, calling God Father while continuing in evil. Some see in it also the language a truly renewed heart will one day use (compare 3:19). Shared ground: both traditions note that the words are ambiguous in context and agree that true return must match lips and life.

verses.text: “ ‘Will he retain his anger forever? Will he keep it to the end?’ Behold, you have spoken and have done evil things, and have had your way.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD quotes the people: “Will he retain his anger forever?” and then sets the quotation against their conduct, “you have spoken and have done evil things.” Arminian readers see presumption here: Judah counts on divine patience while persisting in sin, misusing the very mercy that is meant to lead to repentance (compare Romans 2:4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same presumption as a mark of an unconverted heart that treats God’s mercy as permission. They stress that God’s patience is real but never indifference to sin. Shared ground: both traditions read 3:5 as a warning against confident words without changed ways, and both note that the LORD answers this very question in 3:12.

verses.text: Moreover, the LORD said to me in the days of Josiah the king, “Have you seen that which backsliding Israel has done? She has gone up on every high mountain and under every green tree, and has played the prostitute there.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah reports that the LORD spoke to him in Josiah’s days, asking whether he had seen what backsliding Israel did on every high mountain and under every green tree, the sites of idolatrous worship. Arminian readers note that Israel’s history is presented as a warning Judah could have heeded, which assumes that Judah was able to learn from it and change course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself interprets history for his prophet, showing that he governs the story of both kingdoms and judges it rightly. Shared ground: both traditions read “backsliding Israel” as the northern kingdom, take the dating to Josiah’s reign as Jeremiah’s own framing, and see the high places as covenant betrayal, described soberly.

verses.text: I said after she had done all these things, ‘She will return to me;’ but she didn’t return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I said … ‘She will return to me;’ but she didn’t return.” Arminian readers see a sincere divine expectation that Israel did not meet, showing that God’s appeals can be resisted. Many classical Arminians add that the language expresses the reasonable hope God’s patience had for Israel, without denying his foreknowledge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers usually read the words as the LORD speaking in human terms of the reasonable expectation his kindness warranted, not as surprise at an unforeseen outcome. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God knows all things, that his appeals are sincere, and that Israel’s failure to return was her own fault, witnessed by her sister Judah.

verses.text: I saw when, for this very cause, that backsliding Israel had committed adultery, I had put her away and given her a certificate of divorce, yet treacherous Judah, her sister, had no fear, but she also went and played the prostitute.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he put Israel away with a certificate of divorce, commonly read as the fall of Samaria and the exile under Assyria (2 Kings 17). Arminian readers stress that Judah saw this judgment and still had no fear, which shows real, culpable unbelief: the warning was clear, sufficient, and ignored, and judgment followed as a just consequence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the certificate of divorce God’s just act of judgment on covenant breaking, and in Judah’s fearlessness the hardness that example alone cannot cure. Shared ground: both traditions take the divorce imagery as covenant language for national judgment, not a statement about every individual Israelite, and both see Judah held accountable for what she saw.

verses.text: Because she took her prostitution lightly, the land was polluted, and she committed adultery with stones and with wood.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel took her prostitution lightly, polluting the land and committing adultery with stones and wood, that is, with idols. Arminian readers emphasize the moral seriousness of treating sin lightly: casual unfaithfulness hardens the heart over time, and the verse calls readers to take idolatry seriously while repentance is still possible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the lightness of Israel’s sin the deadness that does not feel its own guilt, a condition only grace can awaken. They note the irony that a living God is exchanged for stone and wood. Shared ground: both traditions read stones and wood as idols, as in 2:27, and keep the imagery covenantal and non-graphic.

verses.text: Yet for all this her treacherous sister, Judah, has not returned to me with her whole heart, but only in pretense,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah has not returned with her whole heart, but only in pretense. Arminian readers note that outward reform without inward turning is not true repentance, and they see the LORD calling for wholehearted response that grace makes possible. Many link this, with some caution, to a reform under Josiah (2 Kings 22–23) that did not reach the people’s hearts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here the limits of external reform: even a godly king’s measures could not create a new heart, pointing toward the promise of 31:33. Shared ground: both traditions hold that God looks for repentance of the whole heart, and both treat the link to Josiah’s reform as a plausible but hedged historical reading.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Backsliding Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah that backsliding Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Arminian readers see greater accountability for greater light: Judah had Israel’s example and the temple, yet fell anyway. Comparative righteousness is not innocence, but it shows that responsibility grows with privilege and warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the comparison as a rebuke to Judah’s presumption on her privileges, not a commendation of Israel. They note that the LORD’s verdict prepares a surprising mercy toward the very kingdom he judged. Shared ground: both traditions read “more righteous” as relative, and see the verse as setting up the call to return in 3:12.
